claim: For the binary LCD code \(C\) of parameters \([57,8,25]_2\) displayed by Lim, An, and Kim (arXiv:2609.02096v1), expand each hexadecimal digit into four binary digits in most-significant-bit-first order and delete the three appended zero columns. Among all \(\binom{57}{2}=1596\) double punctures of this displayed representative, exactly four coordinate pairs—\(\{9,18\}\), \(\{10,30\}\), \(\{34,48\}\), and \(\{41,42\}\), with coordinates numbered from \(1\)—produce an LCD code of minimum distance \(24\). Hence a binary LCD \([55,8,24]_2\) code exists. Since the general binary linear-code bound gives \(d(55,8)=24\), it follows that \(d_{\mathrm{LCD}}(55,8)=24\). This improves the value \(23\) reached at length \(55\), dimension \(8\), in the source's reported shortest-embedding experiments to the sharp bound \(24\).

correctness.rationale: The source matrix was reconstructed from its hexadecimal display and independently reproduced rank 8, Gram rank 8, and minimum distance 25. All 1596 double punctures were enumerated. For each surviving dimension-eight puncture, Gram rank and all 255 nonzero codeword weights were computed exactly over GF(2). Exactly four punctures are LCD with distance 24. The explicit witness has Gram rank 8 and exact weight enumerator 1+49z^24+98z^26+53z^28+9z^30+10z^32+28z^34+7z^36+z^38. Grassl's exact unrestricted [55,8] bound 24 then forces d_LCD(55,8)=24.

value.rationale: The finding closes a natural exact parameter gap explicitly left between a sharp upper bound 24 and the recent source's achieved value 23. It does so by a simple but non-obvious structural operation on the source's new optimal [57,8,25] code and classifies every double puncture of that representative. The one-unit improvement is mathematically decisive because it changes the status of d_LCD(55,8) from bounded to exact, rather than merely improving a heuristic score.
